prompt: A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. A solid flat sun yellow plane covers the entire poster like a printed sheet. Cut out of this yellow plane, filling the upper two-thirds, are two gigantic heavy bold sans-serif characters, "N1", so tall that the top of the N is cut off by the top edge of the poster. The letters are windows with razor-hard edges: through them you see a black-and-white halftone photograph, with a coarse visible halftone dot, of the row of old departure clocks above the main entrance of Flinders Street Station in Melbourne, the round white clock faces with black hands in a long row under the arched entrance, the stone and the tiled steps below, at night under street lamps. The photograph is seen only through the shapes of the letters N and 1; there is no feathering, blending or vignette at the cut. Along the right side of the 1, the yellow plane is notched with two sharp angular arrow-shaped cuts pointing up into the clocks. Below the letters, set in black heavy bold sans-serif on the yellow, large and left-aligned: "UNDER THE CLOCKS". Beneath that, smaller in black: "FLINDERS ST". Inks: sun yellow, black, and the greys of the halftone photograph only. Flat screen print, no gradients on the yellow, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows. Every word spelled exactly: "N1", "UNDER THE CLOCKS", "FLINDERS ST". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks on uncoated off-white paper, four inks at most: kelly green, black, sun yellow, and the off-white of the paper. The whole ground is solid kelly green. The subject is a tram depot at night, drawn in true isometric at 30 degrees: verticals stay vertical, parallel edges stay parallel, no vanishing point. The depot is a long low shed with a sawtooth roof, its roof planes solid black, its walls the off-white of the paper, its shadow sides solid black hard-edged planes. The front wall of the depot is built out of three huge heavy bold sans-serif words, "ONE STAYS UP", standing as solid off-white letter-blocks with black extruded sides; the lettering is skewed onto the isometric face of the wall, so the words are the wall itself and the depot roof rests on top of the letters. Through the open depot bays you see eight trams parked side by side in their tracks, each drawn as a plain black box with a row of black windows: asleep. One tram is different: a sun yellow tram with a row of off-white windows, rolling out of the last bay along black rails, its nose crossing the bottom right edge of the poster and cut off by the frame. Depth comes only from hard-edged solid black shadow planes. No gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows, no light beams from the tram, no stars, no moon, no sky. The headline "ONE STAYS UP" must be readable from across a street. No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no people.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks on uncoated off-white paper, four inks at most: signal red, cobalt blue, black, and the off-white paper as the ground. Four huge heavy bold black sans-serif words are stacked down the poster, left-aligned, filling the width, one word per row in this order: "BAR", "BAKERY", "WARD", "BED". Each word has a solid cobalt blue extruded side dropping down and to the right, a hard-edged flat shadow plane, so the words stand like four blocks of a building. One single transit-map line in signal red, of one fixed thick width, enters from the top edge of the poster and runs down through the four words, bending only at 90 and 45 degrees with one consistent corner radius. It passes through the letters, and at each word it stops at a station: a white circle with a thick black ring placed exactly inside the closed hole of a letter: inside the hole of the A in BAR, the hole of the A in BAKERY, the hole of the D in WARD, and the hole of the D in BED. After the station in BED the red line runs straight down and leaves through the bottom edge of the poster. In the top right corner, small but bold, the line's name "N7" in black inside a signal red circle. Flat vector screen print, crisp edges, no gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows; depth only from the hard-edged cobalt extrusions. Every word spelled exactly: "BAR", "BAKERY", "WARD", "BED", "N7". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no people, no map texture.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks, four inks at most: deep ultramarine blue as the solid ground covering the whole poster, off-white, black, and sun yellow. A single tram-stop sign stands like a tower, its square post rigidly vertical, rising from the bottom edge (the base is cut off by the bottom of the frame). Near the top, two long flat arrow-shaped arms project from the post in opposite directions, one pointing left, one pointing right, slightly tilted at different angles. The left arm carries the heavy bold black sans-serif words "BOTH WAYS" on its off-white face; the right arm carries "ALL NIGHT" on its off-white face; the lettering is printed on and follows the plane of each arm. The upper arm is so long its arrow tip is cropped by the right edge of the poster. Every face is a flat plane of one ink: off-white lit faces, black shadow faces, drawn as an impossible object: the left arm's black shadow side is on its bottom, the right arm's black shadow side is on its top, a deliberate contradiction of light, drawn perfectly cleanly, like an optical illusion. On top of the post sits a small sun yellow rectangular plate with a simple black tram pictogram. At the foot of the post, very small, under one-tenth of the poster's height, one tiny person built from simple geometric shapes: a sun yellow coat, black trousers, a circle head, standing and waiting. Hard-edged shapes, flat vector screen print, no gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows, no stars, no moon, no street lamps. Every word spelled exactly: "BOTH WAYS", "ALL NIGHT". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks, four inks at most: black as the solid ground covering the whole poster, sun yellow, signal red, and off-white. Drawn as a flat side elevation, like an engineering drawing, no perspective. Across the upper third of the poster, one straight overhead tram wire runs horizontally from the left edge to the right edge, a sun yellow line of one fixed width. Above it, a second thinner sun yellow catenary wire sags gently between the two edges. Between the two wires hang huge heavy bold sans-serif letters in off-white, reading "LIVE TILL 5", each letter fixed to the catenary above and to the contact wire below, so the letters are the hangers that hold the wire up; the wire visibly passes through the bottom of each letter. Each letter has a hard-edged flat signal red shadow plane on its right side. Below, in the lower half, a long signal red tram seen exactly side-on: a flat red body with a row of square off-white windows and black wheels on a single black rail line at the bottom; its front runs out past the right edge of the poster and is cut off by the frame. From its roof a black diamond-shaped pantograph rises straight up and touches the yellow wire exactly under the "5". Flat vector screen print, crisp edges, no gradients, no glow, no sparks, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows, no sky, no moon, no buildings. Every word spelled exactly: "LIVE TILL 5". No other text, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text, no people.

A finished graphic design poster, seen flat-on and full bleed; the image is the poster itself, not a mockup on a wall. Printed in flat solid inks on uncoated off-white paper, four inks at most: signal red, cobalt blue, black, and the off-white paper as the ground. A flat transit-map diagram of central Prague. Down the left side runs the Vltava river as a broad solid cobalt blue band of one width, bending only at 45 and 90 degrees, entering at the top edge and leaving at the bottom edge. Several black transit-map lines of one fixed width enter from the top, bottom and right edges and all converge on one single large station, a white circle with a thick black ring, placed right of centre: beside it, in heavy bold black sans-serif, the station name "LAZARSKÁ". The new line is in signal red, the same fixed width but drawn huge: its track bends only at 90 and 45 degrees with one consistent corner radius and lays out the two giant digits "90" across the middle of the poster, the 9 and the 0 built entirely from the red track like rectilinear loops, filling most of the width. The red track starts at the left edge, draws the 9, crosses the cobalt river on a short black bridge, draws the 0, and ends at the LAZARSKÁ station ring, with three smaller black-ringed stations along the way. The digits "90" must be readable from across a street. Flat vector screen print, crisp edges, no gradients, no glow, no gloss, no bevels, no soft shadows, no street texture, no buildings. Every word spelled exactly, with the accent on the A: "90", "LAZARSKÁ". No other text, no other station names, no small print, no logos, no placeholder text.
